newsitem.title: GERMANY: VAT hike idea heats German debate over tax reform.
newsitem.headline: VAT hike idea heats German debate over tax reform.

text.p: A government commission rewriting Germany's tax code drew sharp criticism on Tuesday for planning a rise in value added tax, even though it will not officially reveal its proposals for another week.

After the commission's penultimate meeting on Monday, commission sources said the group might recommend boosting VAT one percentage point to offset part of a planned 70 billion marks ($44 billion) in income and corporate tax cuts.
The Taxpayers' Alliance (BdS) on Tuesday blasted the idea of raising one tax to cut another, calling the proposed VAT increase scandalous.
"With the VAT increase, once again the politicians sneak out of the responsibility for financing tax reform and budget savings," BdS president Karl Heinz Daeke said.
"The positive growth and employment effects of tax reductions would be ruined by a rise in VAT," he said.
Chancellor Helmut Kohl is banking on massive tax reform to stem tax cheating and lift an economy plagued by record unemployment.
His centre-right coalition's tax committee plans to unveil its proposal on January 23, although the proposal's outline has already leaked out.
Committee sources said the top tax rate was likely be cut to 39 percent from 53 percent, short of the coalition's goal of a 35 percent top rate.

Finance Minister Theo Waigel indicated on Tuesday that plans to cut income tax rates to between 19 and 39 percent were within the target zone. "That is in the region that the (coalition parties) have been aiming for," he told reporters.
Coalition sources said the tax reform commission was choosing between a progressive tax scale from 19 to 39 percent and one with five tax brackets between 10 and 39 percent.
Waigel said recently that the two models would bring in roughly the same revenues.
To offset the reductions partly, Bonn has already earmarked 33 billion marks in tax breaks and loopholes for elimination.
A one percent VAT hike would bring in 15 billion marks to cushion the blow to state coffers, commission sources told Reuters.
But opposition Social Democrats (SPD) joined the taxpayer group in attacking the idea.

"The coalition can say goodbye to the idea right now, it has no chance of coming about," SPD chief Oskar Lafontaine said. "The proposal to raise VAT to cut top tax rates makes no sense economically or in terms of fair distribution of wealth."
The commission was also looking at taxing pensions and life insurance payouts -- ideas also opposed by the SPD.

"We would not cooperate in raising taxes on social security recipients, pensioners, the unemployed and middle income earners -- just so that a tax present can be made to high earners," Lafontaine said.

Other proposals discussed in the commission would scale back deductions for commuting costs and lower the top corporate tax rate to 35 percent. German corporations pay 65 percent of undistributed profits in taxes, more than any other industrial country, according to the Institute of the German Economy (IW).

The commission also wants the top tax rates levied on single people making less than 100,000 marks per year. The current 53 percent bracket kicks in for single people earning 120,000 marks or more per year.
